title: How to Reconcile Syncee Supplier Invoices Against Store Payouts Each Month
excerpt: Supplier invoices, marketplace charges and store payouts almost never land on the same day. This monthly routine shows how to match Syncee order costs to the cash that actually reached your bank, and where margin quietly leaks.
body: A supplier invoice, a marketplace charge and a store payout all describe the same order, and they rarely arrive on the same day. That gap is where margin leaks. A dashboard that counts orders will happily report a profitable month while the bank account says otherwise, because the dashboard counts revenue when an order is placed and the bank counts cash when a payout lands. Reconciling the two is a thirty minute job once a month, and it is the difference between guessing at your margin and knowing it.

Pull three things for the same date range: the Syncee order export with product cost and shipping per line, the supplier invoices or statements for that period, and the payment processor payout report. Keep them as separate tabs in one spreadsheet instead of merging the exports into a single view, because you want to see where the numbers disagree, not a blended average that hides the disagreement. Lock the header row and the currency column so a stray sort cannot silently reorder your work.

Match on the order reference, never on the total. Totals collide constantly: two customers in the same week can order the same bundle, and a partial refund can make two different orders look identical. Order level matching also survives split shipments, which become common as soon as a basket includes items from two suppliers. Where a marketplace reference differs from the supplier reference, build the mapping column once and reuse it every month instead of re-solving the same puzzle from scratch.

Expect three specific gaps. The first is currency: a supplier billing in euros against a store selling in dollars will show a variance that is really an exchange rate moving between charge and settlement, and that gap belongs on a finance line rather than in a supplier dispute. The second is shipping billed separately from product cost, which hides freight in a second invoice. The third is app and platform fees that never appear on an order at all, so a per order margin can look healthy while the month does not.

Add a variance column and a tolerance. One to two percent of order value absorbs rounding and rate movement; anything above that gets a note and a follow up. Sort by variance at the end of the pass so the ten worst orders are the only ones you investigate. In practice a handful of orders explain most of the drift, and the usual causes are a manual price override, a cancelled line that got billed anyway, or a supplier swap someone made quietly to keep a delivery promise.

Close the loop by writing the finding back into pricing. If two suppliers have drifted above your target landed margin for three months running, the listing price or the supplier choice is wrong, not the spreadsheet. Name the file with the month and keep the template versioned so next month starts from a known state. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current supplier shortlist with ratings and pricing, and /tool/syncee covers the sourcing side of the same workflow.
